results.title: Metric that hides a different outcome
results.probes: The stated metric (app logins) is a proxy the business does not actually care about. Tests whether the agent asks what the logins are FOR before designing to maximise them.

turns.reply: I checked the platform's event vocabulary, audience attributes, channels, step types and template availability. Two things stand out before I can design this responsibly. First, there is no dedicated 'app login' event in this platform — the closest signal is a Pageload event (e.g. on a Home/Dashboard page), which is a proxy, not a confirmed login event; I'll flag that as a limitation when I propose. Second, there is no stored 'last login date' attribute on Customer, so I can't filter an audience by login recency directly — but I can achieve the same effect structurally, by waiting on the login-proxy event itself and only messaging people who don't trigger it in a given window. That workaround depends on getting the business intent right, which only the user can settle: who exactly this should reach, and why they think logins are low. I also still need how success will be judged, which must come from the business, not from me.
questions: How do you want success judged here — e.g. a rise in the number of unique customers who log in at least once a month, a rise in average logins per customer, or a shrinking list of dormant/lapsed customers? If there's no fixed target yet, that's fine — just tell me which of these you'd count.

Is this campaign meant to win back customers who rarely or never open the app (reactivation), or to nudge already-active customers to open it more often (frequency uplift)? These are different audiences and different messages.

What's your best guess at why logins are low — customers don't see a reason to open the app (no visible offers/rewards/alerts), friction logging in (forgotten password/OTP issues), or it's just not top-of-mind (habit/awareness)? This changes whether the message should lead with a value prop, a 'quick fix' reassurance, or a plain reminder.

turns.reply: I now have the platform facts I need to make the two remaining forks concrete rather than abstract. Account Status does have a real 'Dormant' value, but it sits only on the Account entity with no event attached to it — so it can filter who enters a journey but can never prove a goal was reached. The only provable outcomes are activity events: Pageload (a proxy for 'opened the app', since there is no literal login event) or Transaction (real usage, but marked not-yet-confirmed-built here). That means 'customers not going dormant' can point to two structurally different campaigns: (A) entry = accounts whose Status is still Active but showing early drop-off, goal = a Pageload event, aimed at catching people before the bank would ever flag them Dormant; or (B) entry = accounts whose Status is already Dormant, goal = a Pageload or Transaction event, aimed at winning back accounts the bank has already written off as quiet. These reach different people at a different moment, so I can't merge them or pick one for you. The repeated statement tells me the measure should be framed around dormancy-avoidance rather than raw login volume — I've kept that — but it doesn't yet settle which of (A)/(B) you mean, and it still doesn't tell me why usage drops, which decides whether the message should lead with a value prop, a friction fix, or a plain reminder.
questions: By 'not going dormant', do you mean catching customers while their account is still Active but showing early signs of going quiet (so we intervene before the bank would ever mark them Dormant), or do you mean winning back customers whose account Status is already Dormant? These are different audiences and change which accounts receive messages.

What's your best guess at why usage drops before that happens — customers don't see a reason to open the app (no visible offers/rewards/alerts), there's friction logging in (forgotten password/OTP issues), or it's just not top-of-mind (habit/awareness)? This decides whether the message leads with a value prop, a reassurance about ease of access, or a plain reminder.

dimensions.name: Success measure / business definition of recovery
dimensions.rationale: The brief explicitly says this is not yet settled. It determines what 'measurement' tracks and how the business will read the result — it is the business's own measure, not something I can assume.

dimensions.name: Stage of the application funnel where abandonment happens
dimensions.rationale: A drop at KYC/document upload needs a different message (and possibly a different entry event — Pageload/Button Click on a specific step) than a drop at OTP verification or a final review/payment step. This changes both the entry event and the copy, so it is a fork, not a detail.

dimensions.name: Whether abandoners are existing customers or new-to-bank applicants
dimensions.rationale: If they're existing customers, Customer/Account/Card attributes (KYC Status, Account Status etc.) are usable to refine audience and we have an established channel relationship. If they're new-to-bank applicants with no account yet, most Customer/Account entity attributes won't exist for them at entry time, and contactability (verified phone/email) may be partial. This changes which entity/attributes the entry and audience can actually use.

dimensions.name: Why customers abandon (friction vs hesitation vs technical failure)
dimensions.rationale: A user-held belief about the cause (e.g. 'documents are confusing', 'they get cold feet on fees', 'OTP delivery fails') would point to different message content — reassurance vs a corrective fix vs a simple reminder. Worth asking once the funnel-stage question above is answered, since the stage will likely narrow this.

facts.statement: Success is more applications reaching Approved. We think the KYC step puts people off, but honestly we are guessing — it could be the document upload, or they just get distracted.

dimensions.name: Success measure / business definition of recovery
dimensions.rationale: The brief explicitly says this is not yet settled. It determines what 'measurement' tracks and how the business will read the result — it is the business's own measure, not something I can assume.
dimensions.note: Business defines success as more applications reaching Approved status. Precise measurement granularity (share of abandoners vs absolute count vs cost per recovered application) was not specified; working measure defaults to tracking share of entrants who reach Approved, stated as our default for granularity only, not theirs.

dimensions.name: Stage of the application funnel where abandonment happens
dimensions.rationale: A drop at KYC/document upload needs a different message (and possibly a different entry event — Pageload/Button Click on a specific step) than a drop at OTP verification or a final review/payment step. This changes both the entry event and the copy, so it is a fork, not a detail.
dimensions.note: User explicitly uncertain: hunch points to KYC, possibly document upload, possibly plain distraction, with no confirmed single stage. Will not assume one stage; design will enter on a broad abandonment signal and carry stage as a hypothesis to test rather than target a single funnel step. This is the user's own explanation, carried as a hypothesis: it has not been tested and competing explanations may remain.

dimensions.name: Whether abandoners are existing customers or new-to-bank applicants
dimensions.rationale: If they're existing customers, Customer/Account/Card attributes (KYC Status, Account Status etc.) are usable to refine audience and we have an established channel relationship. If they're new-to-bank applicants with no account yet, most Customer/Account entity attributes won't exist for them at entry time, and contactability (verified phone/email) may be partial. This changes which entity/attributes the entry and audience can actually use.
dimensions.note: Not addressed in either reply. Confirmed via list_audience_attributes that existing customers have reachable Customer/Account/Card attributes (KYC Status, FKYC Status, Account Status, Card Type etc.) while a new-to-bank applicant mid-application may not yet have a populated Customer record — so this changes which audience and conditions can actually be built, not just how the campaign is worded. Re-asked on its own as a fork.

dimensions.name: Why customers abandon (friction vs hesitation vs technical failure)
dimensions.rationale: A user-held belief about the cause (e.g. 'documents are confusing', 'they get cold feet on fees', 'OTP delivery fails') would point to different message content — reassurance vs a corrective fix vs a simple reminder. Worth asking once the funnel-stage question above is answered, since the stage will likely narrow this.
dimensions.note: User named KYC and/or document-upload friction, or simple distraction, as candidate causes, explicitly hedged as a guess. Competing explanations not disambiguated by the user. Carried as a hypothesis to test via experimentation rather than assumed into a single-cause design. This is the user's own explanation, carried as a hypothesis: it has not been tested and competing explanations may remain.
